To moor means to secure a floating vessel — a boat, a ship, a yacht, a houseboat, or anything that floats — so that it stays in one place and doesn't drift away. Think of it as the water-world equivalent of parking a car and putting on the handbrake.

When you moor something, you are attaching it to something fixed and stable. This is done using ropes (called mooring lines), chains, or cables. The vessel gets tied to something that cannot move, and as a result, the vessel cannot move either — at least not far.

You can moor a vessel to many different things. A dock or a pier is the most common — a structure that extends into the water from the shore. You can also moor to a bollard (a thick post fixed into a dock or quayside), to a ring bolted into a harbour wall, to the bank of a river, or to a buoy (a floating, anchored marker out at sea). In each case, the rope goes from the boat to the fixed object, holding the boat in place.

There is one special case worth knowing. A vessel can also be moored by dropping an anchor to the seabed. Here, there is no pier or post involved — the anchor digs into the bottom of the water and the chain or rope connecting it to the boat keeps the vessel from drifting. This is still called mooring, even though the boat is not tied to anything on land or at a harbour. The anchor itself becomes the fixed point.
How the verb is used in sentences

The verb works in two ways. First, you can use it with a direct object — you moor something: "She moored the boat to the dock." Second, you can use it without a direct object, where the vessel itself is the subject doing the action: "The ship moored in the harbour for the night." Both are correct and common.

You will also see it very often in the passive form — where the focus is on the boat being in a secured state rather than on the act of securing it: "The yacht is moored outside the restaurant." This simply means the yacht has been tied up and is sitting there, held in place.

Once a vessel is moored, it is described as moored. A moored vessel is not going anywhere — it is stationary, attached, and waiting. The place where vessels are regularly moored, or the ropes and chains used to moor them, are called moorings. So a harbour might have several moorings available for visiting boats. "She secured the boat at her mooring" means she tied it to her designated spot. "Cast off the moorings" means to untie the ropes and release the vessel so it can sail away.

It is important to note that mooring is specific to vessels on water. You would not moor a car, a bicycle, or an aircraft. However, in informal or figurative writing, you may occasionally see it stretched — "he felt moored to his hometown" — meaning he felt anchored to it, unable to leave. This is a metaphorical use, borrowing the idea of being held in place, but the literal and primary meaning always belongs to boats and water.
A simple way to remember it
If a boat is free, it floats wherever the water takes it. To moor it is to end that freedom — to tie it down, lock it in place, give it a fixed address on the water, even if just for a few hours.
